description: Bibliography for the portal. Journal metadata (title, authors, year, journal, volume, pages, DOI) was retrieved from Crossref, not typed from memory; USGS report numbers from the USGS Publications Warehouse; web pages were opened and read on the verified_at date. Records with in_library=true appear in the Research Paper Library with original summaries whose status is stated in summary_status.

records.title: Blue-green algae (Anabaena spiroides) toxicosis in pigs
records.container: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Veterinary case report: clinical signs, necropsy, and microscopy of pond water, vomitus and stomach contents.
records.key_findings: Seven of 26 finishing hogs on a Kentucky farm were affected after drinking pond water dominated by a bloom identified as Anabaena spiroides.
records.limitations: Single case; toxin identity was not measured with modern analytical chemistry.
records.summary: One of very few published records of cyanobacterial poisoning of livestock in Kentucky, linking deaths of farm pigs to a pond bloom.

records.title: Comparison of Protein Phosphatase Inhibition Assay with LC-MS/MS for Diagnosis of Microcystin Toxicosis in Veterinary Cases
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
organisms: Microcystis (toxin source not identified to genus in the Kentucky case)
records.methodology: Comparison of a protein phosphatase inhibition assay with LC-MS/MS on samples from veterinary poisoning investigations.
records.key_findings: Describes the deaths of 15 cattle around two Kentucky ponds in August 2013; microcystin-LR was detected in one pond and in rumen samples, but not in the second pond.
records.limitations: A methods paper; the Kentucky event is one illustrative case rather than a survey.
records.summary: Shows how microcystin poisoning in livestock is confirmed analytically, using a 2013 Kentucky cattle die-off as a case study.

records.title: Cyanobacteria Growth in Nitrogen- & Phosphorus-Spiked Water from a Hypereutrophic Reservoir in Kentucky, USA
records.summary_status: Summary based on a research assistant's reading of the abstract; the portal editor has not read the abstract directly — verify before relying on details.
records.methodology: Laboratory microcosms of reservoir water spiked with nitrogen and/or phosphorus; cyanobacteria tracked as phycocyanin.
records.key_findings: Phosphate alone did not increase cyanobacteria, while added nitrogen did, suggesting phosphorus was not limiting when the water was collected.
records.limitations: Short microcosm experiment from one reservoir and date; the authors call for more robust designs. Published by SCIRP — weigh the venue.
records.summary: A Kentucky reservoir experiment illustrating that the limiting nutrient for cyanobacteria can be nitrogen rather than phosphorus at a given time and place.

records.title: Development of a Risk Characterization Tool for Harmful Cyanobacteria Blooms on the Ohio River
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Bayesian regression models built on 25 years of discharge data for 20 sites along the Ohio River.
records.key_findings: Bloom occurrence and persistence were predicted from antecedent flow conditions, calibrated on the 2015 and 2019 Ohio River blooms.
records.limitations: Flow-only predictors; does not model toxin production.
records.summary: Explains why low, slow summer flows set the stage for the Ohio River blooms that triggered Kentucky advisories in 2015 and 2019.

records.title: Cyanobacteria, cyanotoxin synthetase gene, and cyanotoxin occurrence among selected large river sites of the conterminous United States, 2017–18
records.container: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Report 2021-5121
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.geographic_scope: 11 large U.S. rivers incl. the Ohio River at Cannelton
records.methodology: USGS pilot sampling (2017–18) of cyanobacteria, toxin-synthetase genes and cyanotoxins at large-river sites.
records.key_findings: Toxin-producing cyanobacteria, toxin genes and cyanotoxins occur in large rivers under ambient (non-bloom) conditions; the report notes the 2015 and 2019 Ohio River events that led to advisories in Kentucky and neighboring states.
records.limitations: Two years, few sites; not designed to characterize any single river fully.
records.summary: USGS evidence that cyanobacteria and their toxins are a river issue, not only a lake issue — including on Kentucky's northern border.

records.title: Tracking Toxins: A Pilot Investigation of Cyanotoxins in North-Central Tennessee’s Surface Waters and Wells
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: USGS and Tennessee Dept. of Environment & Conservation sampled 18 sites, including two wells under surface-water influence, every two weeks (Sept 2022–Nov 2024).
records.key_findings: At least one cyanotoxin was detected at every site; the highest levels were in deep reservoirs, and dissolved microcystin was inversely related to Cumberland River water levels.
records.limitations: Tennessee sites — an analog for, not evidence about, Lake Cumberland or Pulaski County waters.
records.summary: The closest published analog to the Somerset area: cyanotoxin monitoring in a karst landscape on the Cumberland River system downstream in Tennessee.

records.title: Nutrient concentration, stoichiometry, and timing of delivery can regulate cyanobacterial dominance and microcystin production in rivers
records.summary_status: Summary based on a research assistant's reading of the abstract; the portal editor has not read the abstract directly — verify before relying on details.
records.methodology: 36-day incubations of Cumberland River water across four nitrogen–phosphorus gradient scenarios.
records.key_findings: Phytoplankton were co-limited by N and P; N-fixing Dolichospermum dominated at very low N:P, while Microcystis dominated when both nutrients were added.
records.limitations: Laboratory incubations of one river's water.
records.summary: Experimental evidence from the Cumberland River that the amount, ratio and timing of N and P shape which cyanobacteria win.

records.title: Concentrations, and estimated loads and yields of total nitrogen and total phosphorus at selected water-quality monitoring network stations in Kentucky, 1979-2004
records.container: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Report 2009-5240
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: USGS analysis of total nitrogen and total phosphorus concentrations, loads and yields at Kentucky monitoring stations, 1979–2004.
records.key_findings: Agricultural basins had higher TN and TP than forested basins, and intensely karst basins had higher median TN and TP than basins with little or no karst.
records.limitations: Historical record; station network does not include small streams such as Allen Branch.
records.summary: The statewide baseline for nitrogen and phosphorus in Kentucky streams, with explicit comparison of karst and non-karst basins.

records.title: Nutrients, Select Pesticides, and Suspended Sediment in the Karst Terrane of the Sinking Creek Basin, Kentucky, 2004-06
records.container: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Report 2010-5167
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.geographic_scope: Sinking Creek Basin, western-central Kentucky (Breckinridge/Meade area) — NOT the Sinking Creek in Somerset
records.methodology: Streamflow, nutrient, pesticide and suspended-sediment sampling at seven stations, 2004–06.
records.key_findings: Median nitrite-plus-nitrate was 1.6 mg/L; total phosphorus exceeded 0.1 mg/L in 45% of samples; nutrient concentrations were generally higher in spring and summer, matching fertilizer application periods.
records.limitations: Different watershed from the Sinking Creek that receives Allen Branch in NHD; use it as a karst-agriculture analog only.
records.summary: A detailed USGS study of agricultural nutrients in a Kentucky karst basin — and a reminder to check which of Kentucky's several Sinking Creeks a source describes.

records.title: Changes in groundwater quality in a conduit-flow-dominated karst aquifer, following BMP implementation
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Summary based on a research assistant's reading of the abstract; the portal editor has not read the abstract directly — verify before relying on details.
records.geographic_scope: Pleasant Grove Spring basin, Logan County, Kentucky
records.methodology: Before-and-after monitoring of groundwater quality at a karst spring following agricultural best-management-practice (BMP) implementation.
records.key_findings: Nitrate-N at the spring was essentially unchanged after BMP implementation despite wide enrollment of the watershed.
records.limitations: One spring basin; abstract not read directly by the portal editor — verify against the full text before relying on specific numbers.
records.summary: Kentucky karst evidence that nutrient management can take a long time to show up in spring water.

records.title: Nonpoint pollution of surface waters with phosphorus and nitrogen
records.summary_status: Summary written by the portal editor from general knowledge of this widely cited review; abstract not retrieved — verify against the article.
records.methodology: Review of nonpoint (diffuse) sources of nitrogen and phosphorus to surface waters.
records.key_findings: Agriculture and urban runoff are major diffuse sources of N and P; excess inputs cause eutrophication, and managing diffuse sources requires landscape-scale action.
records.limitations: Review from 1998; later work refined the roles of N versus P.
records.summary: Classic review explaining how fertilizer, manure and urban runoff move nitrogen and phosphorus from land into water.

records.title: Eutrophication of lakes cannot be controlled by reducing nitrogen input: Results of a 37-year whole-ecosystem experiment
records.container: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: 37-year whole-lake fertilization experiment with constant P and decreasing (then zero) N additions.
records.key_findings: Cutting nitrogen inputs favored nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria; N fixation kept biomass proportional to phosphorus, and the lake stayed highly eutrophic.
records.limitations: A small, deep, low-nutrient Precambrian Shield lake; transferability to shallow, turbid or flowing waters is debated (see Paerl et al. 2016).
records.summary: Landmark whole-ecosystem evidence for phosphorus control in lakes — and the source of a long debate about nitrogen.

records.title: It Takes Two to Tango: When and Where Dual Nutrient (N & P) Reductions Are Needed to Protect Lakes and Downstream Ecosystems
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Synthesis of whole-lake experiments, mesocosm studies and nutrient-loading data.
records.key_findings: Reducing P alone has worked in some lakes but not others; HABs are often stimulated more by combined N and P enrichment, so dual nutrient reductions are needed in many systems.
records.limitations: Synthesis; the balance of evidence differs among lake types.
records.summary: The case for managing both nitrogen and phosphorus to control harmful blooms, and the counterpart to Schindler et al. (2008).

records.title: Global analysis of nitrogen and phosphorus limitation of primary producers in freshwater, marine and terrestrial ecosystems
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Meta-analysis of N and P enrichment experiments in freshwater, marine and terrestrial ecosystems.
records.key_findings: N and P limitation were equivalent in freshwater, and simultaneous N+P enrichment produced strongly synergistic responses in all three environments.
records.limitations: Experiments differ widely in scale and duration.
records.summary: Shows that co-limitation by nitrogen and phosphorus is common — the reason this portal avoids 'phosphorus alone' or 'nitrogen alone' explanations.

records.title: A review of the global ecology, genomics, and biogeography of the toxic cyanobacterium, Microcystis spp.
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of Microcystis distribution, toxins, genomics, phylogeny and ecology.
records.key_findings: Blooms documented in at least 108 countries (79 reporting microcystin); genomes are highly dynamic, and toxic and non-toxic strains co-occur.
records.limitations: Review.
records.summary: The standard modern overview of Microcystis, the most common bloom-former in eutrophic lakes and ponds.

records.title: The Abundance of Microcystin-Producing Genotypes Correlates Positively with Colony Size in Microcystis sp. and Determines Its Microcystin Net Production in Lake Wannsee
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Size-fractionation of field colonies with counts, genotyping of microcystin-synthetase genes, and toxin analysis.
records.key_findings: The proportion of microcystin-producing genotypes increased with colony size and largely determined microcystin net production.
records.limitations: One lake, one summer.
records.summary: Field evidence that toxic and non-toxic Microcystis genotypes coexist, so the same-looking bloom can carry very different toxin loads.

records.title: The effects of temperature and nutrients on the growth and dynamics of toxic and non-toxic strains of Microcystis during cyanobacteria blooms
records.summary_status: Draft written from a database-generated synopsis; full abstract not retrieved.
records.methodology: Field surveys and experiments comparing toxic (mcyD-carrying) and non-toxic Microcystis under temperature and nutrient manipulations.
records.key_findings: The abundance of toxic (mcyD) Microcystis predicted microcystin better than total cyanobacteria, total Microcystis or chlorophyll a.
records.limitations: Summary based on a database-generated synopsis, not the full abstract — verify against the article.
records.summary: Why toxin-gene measurements outperform cell counts for predicting microcystin.

records.title: Cyanotoxins in inland lakes of the United States: Occurrence and potential recreational health risks in the EPA National Lakes Assessment 2007
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Nationwide survey (EPA National Lakes Assessment 2007) of cyanotoxins (ELISA) and cyanobacteria.
records.key_findings: Microcystins were detected in 32% of samples, cylindrospermopsins in 4.0% and saxitoxins in 7.7%; cyanobacteria were present in 98% and dominant in 76% of samples.
records.limitations: One summer of sampling; ELISA measures toxin classes rather than individual congeners.
records.summary: The national picture: cyanobacteria are nearly everywhere, and microcystins are detected in about a third of U.S. lakes.

records.title: Cyanotoxin Mixtures and Taste-and-Odor Compounds in Cyanobacterial Blooms from the Midwestern United States
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Bloom sampling with community composition, 13 cyanotoxins (LC/MS/MS and immunoassay) and two taste-and-odor compounds.
records.key_findings: Microcystins occurred in all blooms; community composition was not strongly correlated with toxin occurrence, and toxin mixtures were common.
records.limitations: Blooms only (not non-bloom conditions).
records.summary: Shows that which cyanobacteria dominate a bloom does not reliably predict which toxins are present.

records.title: An overview of diversity, occurrence, genetics and toxin production of bloom-forming Dolichospermum (Anabaena) species
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of Dolichospermum taxonomy, genetics, bloom occurrence and secondary metabolites.
records.key_findings: Dolichospermum is the genus name for most planktonic former Anabaena; it is among the most widespread bloom-formers and commonly produces toxins and taste-and-odor compounds.
records.limitations: Review.
records.summary: Explains the Anabaena → Dolichospermum name change and what is known about this nitrogen-fixing bloom-former.

records.title: A review of the phylogeny, ecology and toxin production of bloom-forming Aphanizomenon spp. and related species within the Nostocales (cyanobacteria)
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of phylogeny, ecology, biogeography and toxin genes of 'Aphanizomenon' species.
records.key_findings: The traditional genus is heterogeneous — at least five phylogenetically distant groups — and its members can produce microcystins, anatoxins, saxitoxins and cylindrospermopsin.
records.limitations: Review; taxonomy still under revision.
records.summary: A clear example of why morphology-based genus names in cyanobacteria keep changing.

records.title: A review of current knowledge on toxic benthic freshwater cyanobacteria – Ecology, toxin production and risk management
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of toxic benthic freshwater cyanobacteria.
records.key_findings: Benthic cyanobacteria produce most known cyanotoxins and have been increasingly linked to animal poisonings; long-term studies of why mats proliferate are few.
records.limitations: Review.
records.summary: Essential background for stream work: in shallow flowing water, the cyanobacteria to look for are often attached mats, not floating scums.

records.title: Toxic benthic freshwater cyanobacterial proliferations: Challenges and solutions for enhancing knowledge and improving monitoring and mitigation
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of ecology, toxin production, monitoring and mitigation of benthic cyanobacterial proliferations.
records.key_findings: Toxic benthic proliferations occur in streams, rivers, lakes and ponds in at least 19 countries; flow and other physical drivers rank high among controlling factors.
records.limitations: Few species and habitats are well studied.
records.summary: The most complete guide to monitoring attached cyanobacterial mats in rivers and streams.

records.title: Wadeable streams as widespread sources of benthic cyanotoxins in California, USA
records.summary_status: Summary based on the article title only; abstract not retrieved — verify.
records.methodology: Statewide stream bioassessment survey including benthic algae and cyanotoxins.
records.key_findings: Wadeable streams were widespread sources of benthic cyanotoxins.
records.limitations: Abstract not retrieved — summary from title and general knowledge; verify against the article.
records.summary: Evidence that small streams, not only lakes, can carry cyanotoxins from attached algae.

records.title: Spatial and temporal variation in microcystin occurrence in wadeable streams in the southeastern United States
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: June 2014 reconnaissance of microcystin (ELISA, limit 0.10 µg/L) in 75 wadeable streams.
records.key_findings: Microcystins were detected in 39% of streams (maximum 3.2 µg/L).
records.limitations: One sampling window; low concentrations; Piedmont, not karst.
records.summary: The nearest U.S. survey of cyanotoxins in small streams — a model for a first Allen Branch study design.

records.title: Rise and fall of toxic benthic freshwater cyanobacteria (Anabaena spp.) in the Eel river: Buoyancy and dispersal
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Field experiments on mat buoyancy under light manipulation.
records.key_findings: Benthic Anabaena-dominated mats floated and sank within minutes, driven by oxygen bubbles from photosynthesis — a mechanism for downstream dispersal.
records.limitations: One river system.
records.summary: Shows how attached stream mats detach and float, which matters for where samples should be collected.

records.title: Effects of cyanobacterial toxicity and morphology on the population growth of freshwater zooplankton: Meta‐analyses of laboratory experiments
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Meta-analyses of 597 laboratory comparisons of zooplankton fed cyanobacteria versus nutritious algae.
records.key_findings: Cyanobacteria were poor food relative to small green algae and flagellates; filamentous forms were better food than single-celled (often toxic) forms in these experiments.
records.limitations: Laboratory studies; many used one Daphnia species unexposed to cyanobacteria.
records.summary: The quantitative baseline for 'cyanobacteria are bad food' — and its surprises.

records.title: Meta-analysis of cyanobacterial effects on zooplankton population growth rate: species-specific responses
records.summary_status: Draft written from a database-generated synopsis; full abstract not retrieved.
records.methodology: Meta-analysis of cyanobacterial effects on zooplankton population growth rate by species.
records.key_findings: Responses were strongly species-specific; general support for toxicity or mechanical interference as the main mechanism was not found.
records.limitations: Summary from a database-generated synopsis — verify against the article.
records.summary: Different grazer species respond very differently to the same cyanobacteria.

records.title: The interaction between cyanobacteria and zooplankton in a more eutrophic world
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of laboratory and field studies of cyanobacteria–zooplankton interactions.
records.key_findings: Despite poor food quality and defenses, blooms often coexist with abundant small-bodied zooplankton; grazer responses are diverse and flexible.
records.limitations: Review.
records.summary: Moves beyond 'Daphnia vs. cyanobacteria' to the whole zooplankton community.

records.title: Gene expression and activity of digestive proteases in Daphnia: effects of cyanobacterial protease inhibitors
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Activity-stained gels and gene-expression analysis of Daphnia digestive proteases after exposure to cyanobacterial protease inhibitors.
records.key_findings: Nine digestive proteases were detected in D. magna; exposure to cyanobacterial protease inhibitors changed protease expression and activity, a physiological response to dietary inhibitors.
records.limitations: Laboratory clone and diets.
records.summary: Shows that cyanobacterial compounds act on Daphnia's digestive enzymes, and that Daphnia responds physiologically.

records.title: Protease activity in gut of Daphnia magna: evidence for trypsin and chymotrypsin enzymes
records.container: Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part B: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Biochemical characterization of gut protease activities.
records.key_findings: Trypsin and chymotrypsin activities accounted for most proteolytic activity in Daphnia gut contents — the enzymes targeted by cyanobacterial protease inhibitors.
records.limitations: Enzyme characterization only.
records.summary: Identifies the digestive enzymes that cyanobacterial inhibitors interfere with.

records.title: Rapid evolution revealed by dormant eggs
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Draft written from a database-generated synopsis; full abstract not retrieved.
records.methodology: Hatching Daphnia from dated dormant eggs in sediment and testing resistance to dietary cyanobacteria.
records.key_findings: Mean resistance of Daphnia genotypes to dietary cyanobacteria increased during the lake's eutrophication.
records.limitations: Summary from a database-generated synopsis — verify against the article.
records.summary: 'Resurrection ecology' evidence that grazers can evolve tolerance to cyanobacteria within decades.

records.title: Local adaptation of Daphnia pulicaria to toxic cyanobacteria
records.summary_status: Summary based on the article title and editor's knowledge; abstract not retrieved — verify.
records.methodology: Comparison of Daphnia populations from lakes with different histories of toxic cyanobacteria.
records.key_findings: Daphnia from lakes with high Microcystis exposure tolerated toxic Microcystis better than populations from low-exposure lakes (local adaptation).
records.limitations: Abstract not retrieved; summary from the title and general knowledge — verify against the article.
records.summary: Field-population evidence that naturally tolerant Daphnia exist where toxic cyanobacteria are common.

records.title: Host-genotype dependent gut microbiota drives zooplankton tolerance to toxic cyanobacteria
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Gut-microbiota transplants between Daphnia clones and metagenetic analysis.
records.key_findings: Both host genotype and gut microbiota mediated tolerance to toxic cyanobacteria; tolerance followed the microbiota donor.
records.limitations: Laboratory clones.
records.summary: Evidence that a grazer's gut microbiome can confer tolerance to toxic cyanobacteria.

records.title: Lake restoration by biomanipulation: Round Lake, Minnesota, the first two years
records.summary_status: Summary based on the article title and editor's knowledge; abstract not retrieved — verify.
records.methodology: Whole-lake fish manipulation (biomanipulation) with before-and-after monitoring.
records.key_findings: Early results of removing planktivorous fish to increase large grazers and improve water clarity.
records.limitations: Summary from title/synopsis; abstract not retrieved — verify against the article.
records.summary: An early whole-lake test of biomanipulation, the idea of controlling algae from the top of the food web.

records.title: Biomanipulation as a Restoration Tool to Combat Eutrophication
records.summary_status: Draft written from a database-generated synopsis; full abstract not retrieved.
records.methodology: Review of biomanipulation and related biological restoration methods.
records.key_findings: Biomanipulation can improve water clarity in the short term; long-term stability usually requires nutrient-load reduction and may benefit from combined methods.
records.limitations: Summary from a database-generated synopsis — verify against the chapter.
records.summary: The standard review of biomanipulation as a lake-restoration tool.

records.title: Selective suppression of harmful cyanobacteria in an entire lake with hydrogen peroxide
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Laboratory exposures, in-lake enclosures, then a whole-lake hydrogen peroxide treatment (2 mg/L).
records.key_findings: Dilute H2O2 selectively suppressed cyanobacteria with little effect on eukaryotic phytoplankton, zooplankton or macrofauna in enclosure tests.
records.limitations: Treats the symptom, not nutrient causes; effects are temporary.
records.summary: A carefully staged whole-lake test of a selective chemical treatment — and a model of how to test a control method.

records.title: Mitigating eutrophication nuisance: in-lake measures are becoming inevitable in eutrophic waters in the Netherlands
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Survey of peer-reviewed and grey literature on in-lake interventions against cyanobacterial blooms.
records.key_findings: Many measures (air-bubble or oil screens, surface mixers, low-energy ultrasound, 'effective micro-organisms', fish introduction) had little or no effect; others were more effective but variable.
records.limitations: Dutch shallow lakes; mixed evidence quality.
records.summary: A frank appraisal of which bloom-control products and methods actually work.

records.title: Artificial mixing to control cyanobacterial blooms: a review
records.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Review of artificial mixing studies in lakes and reservoirs.
records.key_findings: Mixing raises oxygen and can shift dominance from cyanobacteria to green algae and diatoms when the mixed depth is large enough; it often fails in shallow systems.
records.limitations: Review; outcomes depend strongly on system depth and design.
records.summary: When aeration and mixing can work against cyanobacteria — and why it often doesn't.

records.title: Genetically engineered organisms and the environment: current status and recommendations
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Ecological Society of America assessment of field-released genetically engineered organisms.
records.key_findings: GEOs could help environmental management, but deliberate or inadvertent releases could have negative ecological effects; recommends case-by-case, science-based risk assessment.
records.limitations: Predates gene-drive technology.
records.summary: The ecological framework for thinking about any proposal to release modified organisms — including grazers or microbes aimed at blooms.

records.title: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms and U.S. Geological Survey science capabilities
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Overview of USGS cyanoHAB science capabilities.
records.key_findings: Major unanswered questions remain about occurrence, environmental triggers for toxicity, and predicting timing, duration and toxicity of blooms.
records.limitations: Overview, not a study.
records.summary: A short guide to how USGS studies cyanobacteria — useful for planning methods.

records.title: Field and laboratory guide to freshwater cyanobacteria harmful algal blooms for Native American and Alaska Native communities
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Illustrated field and laboratory identification guide.
records.key_findings: Provides field images of cyanobacterial blooms and look-alikes (non-toxic algae, floating plants) and guidance on microscopic identification.
records.limitations: Identification guide; toxin production cannot be determined by identification alone.
records.summary: A free, illustrated USGS guide to recognizing cyanobacterial blooms and look-alikes in the field and under the microscope.

records.title: Cyanotoxin occurrence in large rivers of the United States
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Sampling June–September 2017 for cyanobacteria, toxin-synthetase genes and cyanotoxins.
records.key_findings: Cyanobacteria were present in all rivers (82% of samples) but rarely dominated; Pseudanabaena and Planktothrix were most frequent.
records.limitations: One season.
records.summary: Cyanobacteria are routine members of river phytoplankton even when no bloom is visible.

22.1 Prokaryotic Diversity
Harmful Algae Bloom Occurrence in Urban Ponds: Relationship of Toxin Levels with Cell Density and Species Composition
records.container: Journal of Earth and Environmental Science
records.note: PMID 31750421; PMCID PMC6865815. The DOI printed on the PubMed record (10.29011/JEES-148.100048) did not resolve when checked, so it is cited by PMCID.
records.summary_status: Draft summary written from the published abstract; not yet faculty-reviewed.
records.methodology: Year-long monitoring (Oct 2012–Sep 2013) of algal communities, basic water quality and microcystin in several urban retention ponds.
records.key_findings: Blooms were mostly Microcystis and occurred throughout the year; basic water-quality variables (including nitrate and soluble reactive phosphate) did not correlate with cyanobacteria or microcystin, and toxin levels did not always track Microcystis cell counts.
records.limitations: Small number of ponds in one urban area; the DOI listed on the PubMed record does not resolve, so cite by PMID/PMCID.
records.summary: Kentucky evidence that small constructed ponds can host Microcystis blooms year-round and that cell counts are a poor stand-in for toxin concentration.
